newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal denies court ruling shows soft on ETA.
newsitem.headline: Portugal denies court ruling shows soft on ETA.

text.p: Portugal denied on Friday that a court decision to block the extradition of an ETA suspect to neighbouring Spain meant that it was a safe haven for Basque separatist guerrillas.
"Absolutely not. Portugal is committed to adhering to all international extradition laws and applying them," Justice Minister Jose Vera Jardim told Reuters.
But the court's decision was final and there was nothing the Lisbon government could do, the minister added in a telephone interview.

Madrid has reacted angrily to a Lisbon high court ruling denying its request that ETA suspect Jose Luis Telletxea be sent back to Spain to face charges of smuggling rebels and weapons across the country's northern border with France.
Telletxea, 35, arrested in Portugal while trying to board a plane for Venezuela with false papers in 1996, was freed immediately after the court decision on Wednesday.

He had initially been sentenced to six months jail for falsifying documents and his request for political asylum was refused. One day before he completed his term his sentence was increased by three months to enable Portugal to study Spain's extradition request.
Spain, for whom extradition is a highly emotive issue, said that it would be seeking explanations from its neighbour.
When a Belgian court ruled last year against extraditing a couple suspecting of collaborating in an ETA attack, the incident triggered a diplomatic row between Madrid and Brussels.
Belgium's decision to release the pair on political grounds was a slap in the face for Spain, which has demanded an end to the concept of political asylum within the European Union.
But Vera Jardim said that while he did not yet know the full reasons for the court's decision, it would not have been politically motivated.

Portugal had agreed with Spain that the two countries would implement a recent European Union pact on facilitating extradition as soon as their parliaments had ratified it and without waiting for other member countries.
"Portugal has demonstrated great willingness to support... mechanisms of extradition within the European Union," he told Portugal's Antena I radio in an earlier interview.

Nevertheless, a group of left-wing Portuguese politicians and intellectuals, including members of the ruling Socialist Party, recently circulated a petition against the extradition saying that Telletxea could face torture if returned to Spain.

Vera Jardim said that the court could have concluded that Spain had not provided sufficient proof of wrongdoing for the extradition to be granted, but this would only become clear when the ruling was made public next week.

However, Spanish Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal has dismissed such suggestions, saying that the case for extradition was solid. She blamed the decision on a lack of coordination among Portugal's judicial bodies.
